1000023.etyen:
Borrowed from British English Egypt, for various place names in the United Kingdom. The individual British place names arose independently.
The origin of the name in Nailsworth, Gloucestershire, is uncertain. A local-history account records a suggestion that early Egyptian travellers, or possibly people historically identified as “gypsies”, settled beside the river and gave the area its name; the nearby Egypt Mill subsequently took its name from the area. This explanation is not securely established.
The Glasgow name derives from Egypt Farm, also known locally as Little Egypt, at Dalness Stree

en.g: a stepgrandfather or bonus grandfather; a grandparent's new male spouse or partner, or the father of one's stepparent
x: Henning [er] bonusbestefar til Unnis åtte barnebarn
Henning is step-grandfather to Unni's eight grandchildren.

1004631.etyen:
From bonus (“additional family relationship; step-”) + bestefar (“grandfather”). The formation reflects the positive extended use of bonus (“something additional or beneficial”) in family terms, presenting the person as an additional family member rather than emphasizing the absence of a biological relationship.
Compare Danish bonusbedstefar (“step-grandfather, bonus grandfather”), and Swedish bonusmorfar and bonusfarfar (“step-grandfather on the maternal and paternal side, respectively”).

1005143.etyen:
Compound of halleluja (“hallelujah”) + sang (“song”), literally “hallelujah song”.
The first element ultimately derives from Biblical Hebrew הַלְּלוּיָהּ (“praise Yah”), containing the masculine plural imperative of Biblical Hebrew הִלֵּל (“to praise”) and יָהּ (“Yah”), a shortened form of the divine name Biblical Hebrew יהוה (“Yahweh”).
The second element continues Old Norse sǫngr (“song”), from Proto-Germanic *sangwaz (“singing, song”), an o-grade formation ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sengʷʰ- (“to sing, chant”).
